questions.q: A debate topic reads: 'Indian culture only received from other lands and gave nothing back.' Which statement from the chapter best answers it?
questions.a: It adopted or adapted the best of outside currents and also deeply influenced the rest of the world
o: It adopted or adapted the best of outside currents and also deeply influenced the rest of the world
It influenced the rest of the world but adopted nothing at all, which is the reason why it stayed strong
It adopted outside currents only from Greece and Persia, and influenced nobody in return, say some
It influenced other lands only through its religious beliefs and not through arts or science

questions.q: Mahatma Gandhi's lines at the start of the chapter say he wants the cultures of all lands blown about his house as freely as possible but refuses to be blown off his feet by any. Explain in three points how the chapter's description of Indian culture matches this idea.
questions.a: The open windows match the chapter's statement that Indian culture has always been open to external currents and adopted or adapted the best of them. Not being blown off one's feet matches the statement that, unlike the cultures of Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece and Rome, it was not diluted or destroyed but stayed strong. The chapter adds that it influenced the rest of the world through arts, science and philosophy, so the exchange ran both ways.
s: Open windows: adopted or adapted the best of external currents
Not blown off the feet: stayed strong, unlike Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece and Rome
Influence ran outward too: arts, science and philosophy

questions.q:
A student collects four claims about the period and wants to know which the chapter supports.
Claim 1: India has welcomed visitors since ancient times, and they assimilated into society.
Claim 2: Political instability caused disruptions, but culture kept growing richer.
Claim 3: Under the ruling Muslim class in several parts, Persian and Arabic influences often created new art forms.
Claim 4: Like Indian culture, the cultures of Greece and Rome stood strong through the ages.
(a) Which claims does the chapter support?
(b) Correct the claim it does not support.
(c) The chapter calls Indian culture 'remarkably strong and adaptable'. Which claim best shows the 'adaptable' part?
(d) The chapter says it was 'but natural' that Persian and Arabic influences appeared. What does that wording tell you about how the chapter sees these influences?
questions.a: (a) Claims 1, 2 and 3. (b) Claim 4: the chapter says the cultures of Greece and Rome were diluted or even destroyed over time, while Indian culture stood strong. (c) Claim 3: new art forms arose when outside influences met the existing culture. (d) It treats them as a natural result of the ruling Muslim class's patronage in several parts, not as something that overwhelmed local culture.
s: Part (a): claims 1, 2 and 3
Part (b): Greece and Rome were diluted or destroyed
Part (c): claim 3, new art forms
Part (d): a natural result of patronage, not an overwhelming force

questions.q: Farida's cousin says that a village's old lullabies, the rule that guests are fed first and the way elders settle quarrels 'cannot be culture, because culture means only monuments and festivals'. Which reply fits the chapter's meaning of culture?
questions.a: Culture is a group's shared way of life passed down through generations, so values, customs and music count as well
o: Culture is a group's shared way of life passed down through generations, so values, customs and music count as well
Culture is the art and architecture a society has built, so these count only if a ruler patronised them
Culture is the festivals and rituals a group practises, so lullabies and quarrel-settling are everyday habits instead
Culture is whatever a group borrows from visitors, so only practices of foreign origin count

questions.q: A guide at a fort says: 'Egypt, Greece and Rome lost their cultures to others over time, but India's culture has stayed strong because India shut its doors to every visitor.' Which part of her remark conflicts with the chapter?
questions.a: 'Shut its doors to every visitor', since India welcomed visitors from ancient times, who assimilated into society
o: 'Shut its doors to every visitor', since India welcomed visitors from ancient times, who assimilated into society
'Lost their cultures', since the chapter says Egypt, Greece and Rome kept their cultures intact
'Has stayed strong', since the chapter says Indian culture was diluted in the same way as the others over time
'Egypt, Greece and Rome', since the chapter says only Mesopotamia was diluted or destroyed over the centuries

questions.q: Under the patronage of the ruling Muslim class in several parts of the country, a 15th-century court supports a style of painting that mixes local practice with Persian features. Which statement best fits what the chapter says about such developments?
questions.a: Persian and Arabic influences appeared naturally and often produced new art forms
o: Persian and Arabic influences appeared naturally and often produced new art forms
Its deep roots and timeless values
Persian and Arabic influences appeared only in language and never in the arts or architecture
Such influences stayed inside the court and did not touch the culture of the region

questions.q: Karan says: 'Culture grew richer in this period because rulers patronised it. The ordinary people only watched.' Test his claim against the chapter and give a verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. Patronage from rulers of various backgrounds in the arts, languages, literature and philosophy is one of the three patterns the chapter names, so the first half is right. The second half is wrong: the third pattern is active participation by people across all sections of society, so they did not merely watch.
s: First half supported: patronage is one of the three patterns
Second half wrong: active participation by people across all sections
Verdict: partly right

questions.q:
A traveller in the 14th century notes two things in her diary. Note 1: 'The same hymns were sung in this temple this year as in my grandfather's time.' Note 2: 'The new ruler's court hired poets from several regions.'
(a) Which of the chapter's three common patterns does each note show?
(b) Which pattern shows in neither note, and what would she have to observe to record it?
questions.a: (a) Note 1 shows continuation of traditional practices; Note 2 shows patronage from rulers. (b) Active participation by people across all sections of society is missing; she would have to observe ordinary people of every section taking part, for example joining in the singing or the performances.
s: (a) Note 1 continuation, Note 2 patronage
(b) Participation by all sections is missing, and what to observe

questions.q: True or False: Because the chapter says Indian culture continued to grow richer in the 13th to 17th centuries, it claims that political instability caused no disruption at all. Give the reason or correct the statement.
questions.a: False. The chapter says that political instability did create disruptions, yet Indian culture continued to grow ever richer and proved remarkably strong and adaptable.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: disruptions did occur, but culture still grew richer and proved strong and adaptable

questions.q: Your school plans a Culture Fair on this period, with one stall for each of the five dimensions in which the chapter says developments took place. Name each dimension, give one example from anywhere in the chapter that the stall would show, and say in one sentence what the whole fair tells visitors about culture in unstable times.
questions.a: Visual art and architecture: for example Rajput and Mughal miniatures or the Mughal charbagh gardens. Music and dance: for example the qawwali or dhrupad. Language and literature: for example Dhamali songs or Urdu. Science and mathematics: for example Madhava's work toward calculus. Philosophy: for example the bhakti and Sufi traditions. Message: despite instability, Indian culture kept growing richer in all these dimensions.
s: Visual art and architecture stall with a valid example
Music and dance stall with a valid example
Language and literature stall with a valid example
Science and mathematics and philosophy stalls with valid examples
A message that culture kept growing richer despite instability

questions.q: In the imaginary town of Rampur, a chronicler of the 14th century records three things: (i) the weavers' families go on using the same loom methods as before; (ii) the new ruler pays for a school of court musicians; (iii) farmers, potters and traders of every community join the yearly song festival. Which matching of these entries with the chapter's three common patterns is correct?
questions.a: (i) continuation of traditional practices, (ii) patronage by a ruler, (iii) participation by all sections of society
o: (i) continuation of traditional practices, (ii) patronage by a ruler, (iii) participation by all sections of society
(i) participation by all sections of society, (ii) continuation of traditional practices, (iii) patronage by a ruler
(i) patronage by a ruler, (ii) participation by all sections of society, (iii) continuation of traditional practices
(i) continuation of traditional practices, (ii) participation by all sections of society, (iii) patronage by a ruler

questions.q:
A school assembly has a devotional song in a regional language, a rule that elders speak first, and a science exhibition.
(a) Which of the items in the chapter's list of what culture includes does each of the three correspond to?
(b) Using (a), explain in one sentence why the chapter would treat all three as parts of one culture.
questions.a: (a) The song is music, the rule that elders speak first is a custom or value, and the exhibition is science. (b) Culture is the shared way of life of a group passed down through generations, and it includes values, customs and traditions as well as art, music, literature, philosophy and science.
s: (a) Song as music, rule as custom or value, exhibition as science
(b) All are parts of a shared way of life passed down, which culture includes

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter offers only a few vignettes of the cultural life of the 13th to 17th centuries.
Reason (R): India is a vast and diverse country, in which it would be quite impossible to be comprehensive.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: Evaluate how convincing the chapter's claim is that Indian culture is among the most resilient. In five marks: name the four ancient cultures it contrasts India with and what it says became of them, give the four reasons it offers for India's resilience, and judge whether the chapter proves the claim or only states it.
questions.a: The chapter contrasts India with Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece and Rome, which it says were diluted or even destroyed over time. For India it gives four reasons: deep roots, timeless values, scientific temper and rich philosophical and artistic traditions. It also says Indian culture adopted or adapted the best of outside currents. Judgement: the reasons are stated plainly and the contrast is clear, but the chapter only names the other cultures and gives no account of how each declined, so the claim is asserted rather than proved by a worked comparison.
s: Names the four cultures and says they were diluted or destroyed
Gives the four reasons for India's resilience
Mentions openness: adopted or adapted the best of outside currents
Notes the chapter gives no account of how the others declined
Reaches a judgement: asserted more than proved

questions.q:
A Greek scholar, an Arab spice trader and a family fleeing persecution at home each reach India.
(a) Under which kind of visitor in the chapter's list does each fall?
(b) Using (a), state what the chapter says happened to such visitors in India.
questions.a: (a) The scholar is a knowledge-seeker, the trader is a merchant, and the family is among people persecuted in their homeland. (b) India welcomed them and they assimilated into Indian society, benefiting both.
s: (a) Scholar as knowledge-seeker, trader as merchant, family as persecuted
(b) Welcomed and assimilated, benefiting both

questions.q:
(a) State two reasons the chapter gives for the resilience of Indian culture.
(b) Using (a), say which of them a school science exhibition would most directly illustrate.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: deep roots, timeless values, scientific temper, rich philosophical and artistic traditions. (b) Scientific temper.
s: (a) Two reasons from the chapter's list
(b) Scientific temper

questions.q:
Read the statements about the chapter's account.
1. The chapter says Indian culture stayed strong by refusing every external influence.
2. The chapter lists diplomats and people persecuted in their homeland among India's visitors from ancient times.
3. The chapter lists science and mathematics among the dimensions in which developments took place in the 13th to 17th centuries.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
A museum is writing the caption for an exhibit on why Indian culture outlasted several other ancient cultures. Two draft explanations are on the table.
Draft X: 'Indian culture survived because India kept outsiders away, so no foreign influence could dilute it.'
Draft Y: 'Indian culture survived because it had deep roots and timeless values, yet it welcomed visitors and adopted or adapted the best of what they brought.'
(a) Which ancient cultures does the chapter say were diluted or destroyed?
(b) Which kinds of visitor does the chapter say India had from ancient times?
(c) Which draft does the chapter's account of visitors contradict, and in what words?
(d) Choose the draft the museum should print and give the one reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece and Rome. (b) Merchants and traders, knowledge-seekers and scholars, diplomats, and people persecuted in their homeland. (c) Draft X: the chapter says India welcomed the visitors, who assimilated into Indian society, benefiting both. (d) Draft Y: the chapter gives deep roots and timeless values among the reasons and says Indian culture adopted or adapted the best of external currents.
s: Part (a): the four cultures
Part (b): the four kinds of visitor
Part (c): Draft X, India welcomed visitors who assimilated
Part (d): Draft Y, matching the chapter's reasons and openness

questions.q: Neha writes: 'The chapter says developments in this period happened only in visual art and architecture.' Test the claim against the chapter and give a verdict.
questions.a: No. The chapter says developments took place across several dimensions: visual art and architecture, music and dance, language and literature, science and mathematics, and philosophy. Visual art and architecture is only one of them, so the word 'only' makes the claim wrong.
s: Names the five dimensions the chapter lists
Shows 'only' is wrong because art and architecture is just one
Verdict: No

questions.q: A school quiz asks what visitors to India from ancient times brought with them and what became of them. Which answer fits the chapter?
questions.a: They brought their own norms, food, fashion, art and language, and many assimilated, benefiting both
o: They brought their own norms, food, fashion, art and language, and many assimilated, benefiting both
They brought only goods for trade and left again, without any influence on Indian society at all
They brought their cultures but were kept apart from Indian society, so only India benefited from the contact
They came as new rulers whose political systems replaced Indian practices wherever they settled

questions.q: True or False: Political turmoil did not end the recitation of the Alvars' Divya Prabandham and the Nayanars' Tiruvachakam in Tamil homes and temples. Give the reason or correct the statement.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the legacy of the Alvars and Nayanars continued to thrive and the hymns were being recited in homes and temples, showing that cultural currents kept embedded traditions alive while making room for new ideas.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the hymns kept being recited, so embedded traditions stayed alive while new ideas were integrated

questions.q: Raman says: 'The chapter states that the bhakti and Sufi traditions often overlapped, and gives evidence.' Test the claim against the chapter and give a verdict.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says the Bhakti and Sufi traditions often overlapped and that poets brought together ideas from different religions. Evidence: Sufis adopted yogic and Vedantic techniques such as zikr, and Dara Shikoh saw Vedanta and Sufism as converging on universal truth.
s: States that the chapter says they often overlapped
Gives evidence: Sufi adoption of yogic and Vedantic techniques or Dara Shikoh's view
Verdict: Yes

questions.q:
Guru Nanak's teachings are preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib along with the hymns of several Hindu saints.
(a) What message did Guru Nanak spread as he journeyed across regions?
(b) What does the inclusion of the Hindu saints' hymns suggest about how these traditions related?
questions.a: (a) The message of one God and the equality of all people. (b) The traditions overlapped, with ideas shared across religious lines.
s: (a) One God and equality of all people
(b) Inference that traditions overlapped or shared ideas

questions.q: A school poster says: 'The bhakti marga was the one and only path to moksha, and it needed a priest to perform rituals for the devotee.' Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: One of the multiple paths to moksha, needing no rituals or priests at all
o: One of the multiple paths to moksha, needing no rituals or priests at all
It was a path to moksha only for Sufis, and it needed zikr instead of priests
It was one of several paths, but it needed temple rituals led by priests
It was the only path, but it needed no priests once the Puranas were recited

questions.q: The chapter says that more than a millennium after the first encounters with the invaders, India's native belief systems continue and Islam also continues to be practised. Evaluate how far the bhakti tradition, Sufism and the Alvar-Nayanar hymns together support this, and name one limit of the evidence set by the chapter's own account of the invaders.
questions.a: Bhakti saints show native belief growing in popularity through songs of love, compassion and equality. Sufism shows Islam continuing as a devotional, music-centred path that overlapped with bhakti. The Alvar and Nayanar hymns show Tamil devotion continuing, still recited in homes and temples. Together they support coexistence in different regions and traditions. The limit: the chapter also says many invaders sought to annihilate 'infidels', guided by their own version of Islam, causing plunder and destruction of sacred sites, so these traditions do not show that there was no conflict.
s: Bhakti evidence of native belief systems continuing
Sufism evidence of Islam continuing and overlapping with bhakti
Alvar-Nayanar evidence from Tamil Nadu
Judgement that together they support coexistence
Limit: the chapter also records destruction by many invaders

questions.q: A poet born in a family of leather-workers in the early 16th century composed poetry promoting equality and oneness of all, breaking down the walls around varna and jati. The chapter names this poet ___.
questions.a: Ravidas

questions.q: Two verses survive from this period. Verse A speaks of one god and mocks the rituals of both Hinduism and Islam. Verse B argues for the equality and oneness of all and against the rigid walls around varna and jati. Which saints do they most likely come from, going by the chapter?
questions.a: A from Kabir; B from Ravidas
o: A from Kabir; B from Ravidas
A from Ravidas; B from Kabir
A from Guru Nanak; B from Kabir
A from Ravidas; B from Chaitanya Mahaprabhu

questions.q: Sana says: 'Bhakti spread because kings forced everyone to join it.' Test the claim against the chapter and give a verdict.
questions.a: No. The chapter says verses and songs in local languages expressed love, compassion and equality, and people from all sections of society took part in bhajans with music and dance as devotion. It says patronage may have enabled the developments but it was the participation of the people that led to their thriving, and nothing says anyone was forced.
s: Cites local-language songs and voluntary gatherings across society
Cites that participation of the people, not patronage, led to thriving
Verdict: No

questions.q:
The Divya Prabandham of the Alvars and the Tiruvachakam of the Nayanars were composed between the 6th and 9th centuries. They were being recited in homes and temples in Tamil Nadu during the 13th to 17th centuries.
(a) Show that a hymn recited in the 14th century, even if composed as late as the 9th century, was more than four centuries old. (Take the 9th century as ending in 900 and the 14th as beginning in 1301.)
(b) What does the chapter say such continuing hymns show about cultural currents?
(c) According to the chapter, what may the patronage of rulers have done, and what led to the thriving?
(d) A student predicts that the hymns would have faded once rulers of other beliefs held power. Which chapter statement most directly goes against this prediction?
questions.a: (a) 1301 - 900 = 401 years, which is more than four centuries. (b) They kept embedded traditions alive while making room for new ideas to be integrated. (c) Patronage of Hindu and Muslim rulers may have enabled the developments, but the participation of the people led to their thriving. (d) That the legacy of the Alvars and Nayanars continued to thrive, with the hymns still recited in homes and temples.
s: Part (a): 401 years, more than four centuries
Part (b): kept embedded traditions alive while making room for new ideas
Part (c): patronage may have enabled; participation led to thriving
Part (d): the legacy continued to thrive with hymns recited in homes and temples

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with the person or tradition in Column B that the chapter links it to.
Column A: 1. Songs that fuse local classical styles with Sufi ones to bring people closer to the divine  2. Hymns to Shiva still recited in Tamil temples  3. A couplet comparing wheat ground into flour with Ram and Rahim  4. A teacher who journeyed across regions; his teachings are preserved in a sacred text of the Sikhs
Column B: a. Kabir  b. Guru Nanak  c. Qawwalis  d. The Nayanars' Tiruvachakam
A student writes that the chapter blames 'Islam' for the destruction of temples. Using the exact words of the chapter's framing, give two points that show the student has overstated it.
questions.a: The chapter attributes the plunder and destruction to the desire of many of the invaders, guided by their own version of Islam, not to Islam as a whole. It also says that Islam continues to be practised in India along with other religions and native belief systems.
s: Attributes the motive to many invaders and their own version of Islam
Notes that Islam and native belief systems continue side by side

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The renewed popularity of the bhakti tradition in this period reflected society's search for spiritual resilience amid political and religious upheaval.
Reason (R): The bhakti marga required elaborate rituals conducted by priests.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, R is false
o: A is true, R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, R is true

questions.q: In a 16th-century village, people from every section of society gather to sing bhajans with musical instruments and dancing. What does the chapter say such gatherings expressed, and what did some of the bhajans reinforce?
questions.a: Devotion to god; some bhajans reinforced the oneness of god, an idea from the Upanishads and Islam
o: Devotion to god; some bhajans reinforced the oneness of god, an idea from the Upanishads and Islam
Loyalty to the ruler; some reinforced the idea of many separate gods, each for one section of society
Devotion to god; all of them rejected the Upanishads and the idea of a single god in every form
Devotion to god; some reinforced the rituals that only priests could perform in the temple

questions.q: Imran says: 'Sufis were wholly outside India's older traditions; nothing in their practice came from them.' Which detail from the chapter best refutes him?
questions.a: Sufis adopted yogic and Vedantic techniques such as inner silence, asceticism and zikr
o: Sufis adopted yogic and Vedantic techniques such as inner silence, asceticism and zikr
Sufi saints sang qawwalis in praise of Krishna and Shiva in every case
Sufism is described as a path of Islam focused on an inner, personal search
Sufi saints such as Chishti and Nizamuddin Auliya encouraged music in the Sufi tradition

questions.q:
Kabir's doha says that when wheat is ground into flour all distinctions between grains disappear, and in the same way all differences between Ram and Rahim dissolve when one realises the divine.
(a) What idea about god does the doha express?
(b) Using (a), suggest why an everyday image from the kitchen suits a message meant for people of all sections of society.
questions.a: (a) The oneness of god: Ram and Rahim are names of god in Hinduism and Islam. (b) Everyone knows grinding wheat into flour, so the image makes the idea easy to grasp without rituals, priests or learning.
s: (a) The oneness of god, with Ram and Rahim as names in the two religions
(b) A familiar everyday image anyone can understand

questions.q:
A village committee in the 16th century wants a gathering that will bring together people of every community after a bitter quarrel. Three plans are put forward. Plan 1: a recital of ritual texts by priests, open only to those trained in them. Plan 2: a gathering of bhajans in the local language, with instruments and dancing, open to all. Plan 3: a lecture on the differences between the religions.
(a) What is the bhakti marga, and what did it not require?
(b) Name two features of bhakti verses and songs from the chapter that suit Plan 2.
(c) Whose couplet about Ram and Rahim could the committee use to open the gathering, and what does it say?
(d) Which plan should the committee choose? Give the reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The path of devotion, one of the multiple paths to moksha; it did not require rituals or priests. (b) Verses and songs in local languages expressing love, compassion and equality, connecting people through songs, music and dance. (c) Kabir's: when wheat is ground into flour all distinctions between grains vanish, and when one realises the divine all differences between Ram and Rahim dissolve. (d) Plan 2: bhakti needed no rituals or priests and people from all sections took part in bhajans with music and dancing, so it can bring everyone together, while Plan 1 shuts out people and Plan 3 stresses differences.
s: Part (a): path of devotion, no rituals or priests
Part (b): local languages, love, compassion, equality, music and dance
Part (c): Kabir's flour couplet and its meaning
Part (d): Plan 2, because all sections could take part without rituals or priests

questions.q: Two towns in the 15th century are compared. In Town A a ruler funds bhajan singers, but few townspeople join in. In Town B nobody funds the singers, but people of every section sing and dance together at gatherings. The funding ends in both towns. Going by the chapter's reasoning, which town's devotional tradition is more likely to keep thriving?
questions.a: Town B, because patronage may have enabled such developments but the participation of the people led to their thriving
o: Town B, because patronage may have enabled such developments but the participation of the people led to their thriving
Town A, because the chapter says that a ruler's patronage is what makes devotional traditions thrive, with the people's role as only a minor matter
Both equally, because patronage and participation are the same thing
Neither, because bhajans could not survive political turmoil

questions.q: Name two features of bhakti verses and songs in this period that the chapter gives, and explain how they helped connect people.
questions.a: They were composed in local languages and expressed love, compassion and equality. People could understand them in their own speech, and the songs, music and dance connected people across sections of society.
s: Two features: local languages; love, compassion and equality
Explains the connection: understood by all, music and dance brought people together

questions.q:
At a gathering in Delhi, singers sing a local classical tune with words of love, faith and unity, to bring listeners closer to the divine.
(a) What are such songs called in the chapter, and whose tradition were they?
(b) Which two famous saints does the chapter say encouraged music as a way to connect with god?
questions.a: (a) Qawwalis, the devotional songs of Sufi saints, fusing local classical musical styles with their own. (b) Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti and Nizamuddin Auliya.
s: (a) Qawwalis, Sufi devotional songs fusing local classical styles
(b) Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti and Nizamuddin Auliya

questions.q: Write a three-line situation in which a Sufi gathering and a bhakti gathering in the same town overlap, and mark where each of three links the chapter mentions shows: devotion through music, a shared idea, and poets bringing together ideas from different religions.
questions.a: Sample: Qawwali singers and bhajan singers gather in one courtyard, both using music to express devotion. A poet who knows both traditions writes verses that join the idea of one god with the Vedantic idea of oneness. Listeners of both religions sing along, and the poet's themes of unity and devotion enrich local literature. Any situation that shows the three links, labelled, earns the marks.
s: Devotion through music shown in both gatherings
A shared idea such as oneness of god
A poet bringing together ideas from different religions

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Sufis adopted yogic and Vedantic techniques such as inner silence and zikr to achieve spiritual union.
2. Ravidas lived in the 15th century in present-day Uttar Pradesh.
3. People from all sections of society took part in gatherings where bhajans were sung with instruments and dancing.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Compare Kabirdas, Ravidas and Guru Nanak. For each, state from the chapter one point of their message, and then explain what the three have in common that explains why bhakti songs appealed to people across society.
questions.a: Kabirdas, of the 15th century in present-day Uttar Pradesh, spoke of one god and decried the rituals of both Hinduism and Islam. Ravidas, of the early 16th century, promoted equality and oneness of all, breaking the walls around varna and jati. Guru Nanak journeyed across regions spreading one God and the equality of all people; his teachings and the hymns of several Hindu saints are preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib. Common: all stressed oneness and equality and put devotion above ritual, which made the path open to people of every section. Guru Nanak's equality of all is not tied by the chapter to varna or jati, so only Ravidas is credited with that.
s: Kabirdas: one god and decrying rituals of both religions
Ravidas: equality and oneness, breaking varna and jati walls
Guru Nanak: one God and equality, teachings in the Guru Granth Sahib
Common thread: oneness and equality
Link to appeal across all sections of society without rituals or priests

questions.q: Vikram says: 'Amir Khusrau is credited with developing the qawwali by drawing only on Indian singing traditions.' Test the claim against the chapter and give a verdict.
questions.a: No. The chapter says Amir Khusrau, an Indo-Persian Sufi poet and singer, is credited with developing the qawwali as a form of Sufi devotional song fusing Indian, Persian and Arabic singing traditions, so 'only Indian' is wrong.
s: Names him as credited with the qawwali, a Sufi devotional song
Says it fused Indian, Persian and Arabic singing traditions
Verdict: No

questions.q: True or False: Tansen was invited to Akbar's court by Raja Mansingh Tomar, the patron under whom dhrupad developed. Give the reason or correct the statement.
questions.a: False. Raja Mansingh Tomar of Gwalior patronised the development of dhrupad in the late 15th century. Tansen went to Akbar's court at Akbar's insistence and became one of the nine ratnas of his court.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: Tansen went to Akbar's court at Akbar's insistence; Mansingh Tomar patronised dhrupad

questions.q:
Tansen, renowned for his expertise, went to Akbar's court at Akbar's insistence and became one of the nine ratnas. Some of his compositions reflect the influence of a Sufi saint, yet he continued to compose in praise of Krishna and Shiva. Purandaradasa, a devotee of Krishna in the south, had his fame reach Krishnadevaraya's court.
